explanations.answer: Saddled donkeys loaded with food and wine
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, brought a pair of saddled donkeys. They carried two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits and a skin of wine. Those donkeys put in a longer shift than I do on cookie Saturday.

explanations.answer: A band of armed men from Benjamin
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Ziba's cargo in this verse is donkeys, bread, raisins, summer fruit and wine, with no weapons mentioned. Armed men aren't part of what he brings. Ziba came to the road carrying groceries, not swords.

explanations.answer: A message from Hushai in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Close to the neighborhood, but no. Hushai, David's friend (2 Samuel 15:37), went into Jerusalem after David told him to go back to the city (2 Samuel 15:34). This verse doesn't bring up any message from him. What Ziba has is on the donkeys' backs: bread, raisins, summer fruit and wine.

Yes, baker. Ziba says, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride, the bread and summer fruit are for the young men to eat…” He adds that the wine is to refresh those who become exhausted in the wilderness. Donkeys for riding, food for eating, wine for the worn out. I can't even explain my own cookie budget that clearly.

Not quite, friend. Ziba never mentions a priest in his answer. He says the donkeys are for the king's household to ride. The young men get the bread and summer fruit, and the wine is for anyone who becomes exhausted in the wilderness.

Good guess, but no prophet in this answer. Ziba says the donkeys are for the king's household to ride, and the bread and summer fruit are for the young men to eat. The word is king. A prophet would have to wait his turn, and apparently he wasn't even in line.

Right, baker. David asks where Mephibosheth is, and Ziba answers that he is staying in Jerusalem. Then Ziba reports that Mephibosheth has said, “Today, the house of Israel will restore to me the kingdom of my grandfather.” Notice that this is what Ziba says Mephibosheth said.

This one is true, friend. Ziba tells David that Mephibosheth is staying in Jerusalem. He then reports that Mephibosheth has said, “Today, the house of Israel will restore to me the kingdom of my grandfather.” That's the whole report, and it's Ziba's telling of it. It's an easy one to doubt, because those words are a lot to hear on a road like that.

explanations.answer: Gives him all his master's property
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. David tells Ziba, “All that belongs to Mephibosheth is now yours!” That's a big gift to hand out on a dusty road after one short conversation. Ziba answers by bowing and asking, “May I find favor in your eyes, my lord the king!”

explanations.answer: Makes him captain over the guard
explanations.explanation: No promotion in this passage, friend. David doesn't give Ziba a rank or a command. He tells him, “All that belongs to Mephibosheth is now yours!” It's all about the property, and there's no uniform in the deal.

explanations.answer: Sends him back to watch the palace
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. David doesn't send Ziba anywhere in these verses, and nobody gets handed a palace job. What David says is, “All that belongs to Mephibosheth is now yours!” Ziba shows up with donkeys and bread, and he leaves with somebody else's whole estate. I think that's the best delivery run he ever made.

You got it, baker. Shimei son of Gera, a man from the family of the house of Saul, kept yelling out curses as he came closer. He threw stones at David and at all the king's servants. The troops and mighty men were right there on David's right and left, and he threw anyway.

explanations.answer: Bows low and asks for mercy
explanations.explanation: That one belongs to Ziba, friend, and even he didn't ask for mercy. Ziba said, “I humbly bow before you…” and asked to find favor in the king's eyes. Shimei came out of Bahurim with a very different style. He kept yelling out curses and threw stones.

explanations.answer: Warns him that Absalom is coming
explanations.explanation: No warning from Shimei, baker. He shows up yelling curses and throwing stones at David and the king's servants. Absalom is David's son, and Shimei brings him up only inside his yelling. He says the LORD has delivered the kingdom into Absalom's hand (2 Samuel 16:8).

Yes, baker. Shimei yells, “The LORD has paid you back for all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned…” He adds that the LORD has delivered the kingdom into the hand of David's son Absalom. Those are Shimei's words, spoken while he's yelling and throwing stones. Hold onto that, because David has an answer coming.

No prophet in Shimei's yelling, friend. He says it was the LORD who paid David back and delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom. Shimei doesn't point to a prophet at all. He just yells, throws stones and keeps going.

Not a council, baker. Shimei doesn't point to any group or meeting. In his words, “The LORD has paid you back for all the blood of the house of Saul…” He puts the whole thing on the LORD, and those are his words, not a fact the passage confirms.

explanations.answer: Go over and cut off his head
explanations.explanation: That's what he asked, baker. Abishai son of Zeruiah, one of David's men, says, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and cut off his head!” It's a heavy moment, and I think Abishai was ready to act right then. Next comes David's answer.
Abishai wanted more than a chase, friend. He asks David, “Let me go over and cut off his head!” That's serious, and it's a heavy part of the story. Chasing Shimei off isn't what he asks for.
That's not what he asked, baker. Abishai son of Zeruiah doesn't ask to throw anything. He says, “Let me go over and cut off his head!” That's a much heavier request than a rock-throwing contest.

explanations.answer: The LORD may have told Shimei to curse him
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. David says, “If he curses me because the LORD told him, ‘Curse David,’ who can ask, ‘Why did you do this?’…” He doesn't answer Shimei with a fight. He says "if," and leaves room for the LORD to be behind it. That's a lot to say with stones flying at him.

explanations.answer: Saul's family may have sent Shimei out
explanations.explanation: Shimei is from the family of the house of Saul (2 Samuel 16:5), but that's not what David says. David says, “If he curses me because the LORD told him, ‘Curse David,’ who can ask, ‘Why did you do this?’…” His answer points to the LORD, not to Saul's family.

explanations.answer: Absalom may have paid Shimei to do it
explanations.explanation: David never says that, friend. Nothing in these verses says Absalom paid anybody. David says, “If he curses me because the LORD told him, ‘Curse David,’ who can ask, ‘Why did you do this?’…” He leaves it with the LORD.

David goes the other way, baker. He says, “Behold, my own son, my own flesh and blood, seeks my life. How much more, then, this Benjamite!” Then he tells Abishai, “Leave him alone and let him curse me, for the LORD has told him so.” So Abishai doesn't get his go-ahead.
Yes, baker. David says, “Leave him alone and let him curse me, for the LORD has told him so.” That's David turning down Abishai's request. He tells both Abishai and all his servants to let Shimei be.

That's the word, baker. David says, “Perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and repay me with good for the cursing I receive today.” Notice the "perhaps." David isn't demanding anything. He's hoping, with stones still flying.

Nice try, friend, but David says something else. His words are, “Perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and repay me with good for the cursing I receive today.” The word he uses is good. He's talking about being repaid for what he's receiving.

Peace sounds right for that moment, baker, but it's not David's word. He says, “Perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and repay me with good for the cursing I receive today.” He says good, and he starts with "perhaps."

The text says the opposite, friend. When the king and all the people with him arrived, they were exhausted. Remember Ziba's wine was to refresh those who become exhausted in the wilderness (2 Samuel 16:2). After all that walking and all that yelling, I'd be flat on the floor too, like after a double batch.

Right, baker. The king and all the people with him arrived exhausted. And there he refreshed himself. After a road like that, one with curses, stones and dust, I'd need a long sit-down too, probably with my mustache hanging.
